[Source 1 — www.motherjones.com] (URL: https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/10/libs-of-tiktok-raichik-california-ballot-envelope-holes-voter-fraud/):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Libs of TikTok is reviving an old conspiracy theory about California's ballots

The little holes in the envelopes aren’t there to help the state steal your vote.

Actual Article Body:
A vote-by-mail ballot and return envelope mailed to a California resident ahead of the general election, photographed on October 17, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.Jay L. Clendenin/Getty

“California is rigging the elections,” announced the far-right conspiracist account Libs of Tiktok, run by real estate agent-turned-provocateur Chaya Raichik, on Sunday. Her evidence: small holes punched in the state’s ballot return envelopes. Raichik, whose post was viewed by 1.5 million people, shared a video filmed by someone who claimed the holes in the envelope were designed to reveal the vote within.

Similar claims date back to at least 2021, when viral videos began to circulate asserting that the holes would be used for tampering during that year’s gubernatorial recall election. Since then, disinformation like Raichik’s has kept the idea alive.

But the real reason behind the holes is much simpler and less insidious: they’re there so that blind and low-vision people know where to sign their envelopes. During the statewide special elections of November 2025, rumors about the ballot-envelope perforations became so pervasive that the California Secretary of State issued a statement about it:

“We have been seeing a great deal of misinformation about the November 4, 2025, Statewide Special Election ballot envelopes, and I want to set the record straight,” said Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber at the time.

“The small holes on ballot envelopes are an accessibility feature to allow sight-impaired voters to orient themselves to where they are required to sign the envelope,” she said. The holes also help election workers determine whether there’s a ballot inside the envelope, an important consideration when you are trying to count ballots.

The envelope-holes theory isn’t the only conspiracy churning about the California elections this cycle. Federal agencies have alleged without evidence that tens of thousands of noncitizens may be voting in California, the latest unfounded claim of a mass voter fraud ring favoring Democrats. President Donald Trump also claimed in June that progressive Democrat Nithya Raman could not have won her mayoral primary in Los Angeles—and that those elections must have been rigged.

According to an August study by researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, all these stories of pervasive election fraud—be it immigration-related or tiny-holes-in-envelopes-related—have led a full 75 percent of the state’s Republicans to say they are “not confident” in California’s election systems. (Most Democrats, meanwhile, are worried about federal and foreign governments intervening in their elections, as opposed to internal fraud.)

If the holes in your envelope show your vote, some commenters online pointed out, you’re probably folding your ballot wrong.

DAVID MARCUS: California transplants in Texas are voting Democrat, and they see no irony in it

California to Texas migration is reshaping Texas politics as Democratic transplants bring progressive values to the once ruby red McKinney, Texas.

Actual Article Body:
This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. ©2026 FOX News Network, LLC. All rights reserved. Quotes displayed in real-time or delayed by at least 15 minutes. In McKinney, Texas, California transplants explain why they're voting Democrat despite leaving a blue state, as Republicans fear a political shift.

McKinney, Texas, is ground zero for the migration of voters from California to Texas over the past several years. On Election Day, it is these newcomers who may well tip the balance not just in the Senate and governor's races.

They may also decide whether the once ruby red Lone Star State will continue to grow bluer.

I met Oren at The Celt on the picture-postcard town square, where we played a friendly game of pool. He moved from California about a year ago "because it’s a lot cheaper to live" but is voting for Democrats because he believes that Texas needs "more social services and public transit" and more support for transgender kids.

When I gently tried to press Oren on the apparent illogic of moving away from a high-tax, big-government blue state for reasons of cost only to vote to make his new home a high-tax, big-government state, he was unmoved, almost arguing that real California progressivism has never been tried.

Blue state residents are fleeing places like California for red states. (iStock)

FOX NEWS POLL: TEXAS SENATE RACE GALLOPING TOWARD A PHOTO FINISH

It turns out that Oren was not as much of an outlier as I had expected because, not long after, I met Daniel, who works at a local restaurant and moved to McKinney a few years ago with his best friend and girlfriend to start a business. He has also proudly brought his politics with him.

"It’s in the Constitution," Daniel told Fox News Digital. "We can go anywhere we want. It's meant to be that way."

When I asked him if he could understand why so many people born and raised in Texas are worried about transplants changing its politics, he shrugged and said, "Things change."

California is facing an ongoing exodus of residents, taxpayers and businesses to lower-cost states such as Texas. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

JOE ROGAN WARNS LIBERALS AGAINST TRYING TO TURN TEXAS BLUE, SAYS IT WOULD WRECK THE STATE'S 'DELICATE BALANCE'

In the space of about five hours, I met two more refugees from California prepared to keep voting for Democrats. Like Oren and Daniel, they really did not see any irony in the fact that they may be recreating in Texas exactly the conditions they escaped in California.

The natives, however, do see the problem with the Californication of Texas. Terry, a longtime local in her 60s, told me, "I love to see the growth, and there’s a lot of it, but if they bring Democratic politics with them, then we stand to lose the whole thing bringing people here."

Clint, who was in town from his home just on the other side of the Oklahoma border, is worried not just about Texas turning blue through domestic migration, but even about the Sooner State eventually turning blue.

California businesses and taxpayers are increasingly looking elsewhere as high costs fuel an ongoing exodus from the Golden State. (AaronP/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images)

TRUMP WON THIS RELIABLY RED STATE BY DOUBLE DIGITS; NOW A DEADLOCKED RACE IS BRINGING HIM BACK

"I cannot comprehend why someone would move from a state because there’s high taxes and then come down here and vote for high taxes. I just can’t comprehend it," Clint told Fox News Digital. "And I’ve asked them to explain it to me, but they just cuss me out."

Thankfully, nobody cussed out this columnist for asking, but Clint is correct that the liberal transplants see no problem with transforming the red states they arrive in into blue states, and it's not just Texas.

Arizona and even Montana have seen influxes of liberal California voters. West Virginians have similar fears regarding their neighbors to the south in Northern Virginia, who are also attracted by the low taxes and cost of living.

Lower taxes, cheaper housing and affordability concerns have helped fuel population growth across many Southern and Sun Belt states, Census Bureau estimates show. (Robert Daemmrich Photography Inc/Corbis/Getty Images)

ELECTION DAY 2026: JOIN AMERICA'S CONVERSATION HERE!

In Texas, there is a kind of double-pincer political invasion because, along with the Cali converts, unchecked immigration — illegal and otherwise — over decades has also pushed the needle left in the state. This is, in a nutshell, the new Democratic Party coalition: wealthy, college-educated Whites and immigrants.

The bottom line for Republicans — not just in Texas but in many red states — is that Americans are moving at stunning rates to cheaper states, which almost always means Republican states. The good news is that red states stand to gain in the Electoral College and in Congress after the next census, but that won’t matter if Democrats take them over.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Between now and then, and especially on Tuesday, "Don’t you turn my red state blue" has to be the mantra of the GOP. If Texas falls this time, then anywhere can, and that is exactly what the Democrats moving to red states are hoping for and creating.

David Marcus is a columnist living in West Virginia and the author of "Charade: The COVID Lies That Crushed A Nation."

Mpox outbreak hits California county as health officials probe US spread

A host of recent cases of have been reported, raising fresh concerns about possible community transmission.

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

A potentially dangerous strain of mpox has surfaced in California’s Central Valley, with health officials investigating whether the virus is spreading within the US.

Four recent cases of Clade I mpox have been reported in Stanislaus County, raising fresh concerns about possible community transmission of a strain historically associated with international travel.

The California Department of Public Health has confirmed two infections as Clade I, while additional testing is underway to determine whether the remaining two cases involve the same strain, according to Stanislaus County health officials.

The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

Never miss a story

Three of the infected individuals reported no recent international travel, while investigators are still examining the travel history of the fourth patient.

The troubling discovery comes as health authorities investigate a possible shift in how the virus is spreading across the country.

Until recently, Clade I mpox infections in the US were largely associated with people who had traveled internationally. But since August 2026, health officials have identified an increasing number of cases involving patients with no recent overseas travel.

That pattern suggests the virus may now be circulating within US communities, although officials have not established how the individuals in Stanislaus County contracted the infection.

Still, Dr. Thea Papasozomenos, Stanislaus County’s public health officer, stressed that the threat to the broader public remains small.

“While we have identified four cases in our county, we want residents to know that the risk to the general public remains low,” Papasozomenos said. “Being aware of the symptoms, getting vaccinated if at risk of exposure to mpox, and seeking medical care when needed are important ways to protect yourself and prevent the spread of mpox.”

Mpox, formerly known as monkeypox, is a viral infection that can cause painful, blister-like sores and a range of flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headaches and muscle aches.

California Post News: Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X, YouTube, WhatsApp, LinkedInCalifornia Post Sports Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, XCalifornia Post  Opinion California Post Newsletters: Sign up here!California Post App: Download here!Home delivery: Sign up here!Page Six Hollywood: Sign up here!

Some patients develop only a handful of lesions without experiencing other symptoms, making infections potentially harder to recognize.

Symptoms can emerge up to 21 days after exposure, and most infected people recover within two to four weeks. However, the disease can sometimes cause serious complications.

There are two major types of the virus, Clade I and Clade II, both of which spread through similar forms of close contact.

The virus is primarily transmitted through direct skin-to-skin contact, including intimate or sexual contact, as well as exposure to infected sores or bodily fluids.

People can also become infected by sharing contaminated clothing, towels or bedding.

However, officials emphasized that the mpox virus does not spread easily through everyday encounters, such as passing someone at a grocery store or sharing an office.

Health authorities are urging residents at increased risk of exposure to get vaccinated with JYNNEOS, a two-dose vaccine administered approximately four weeks apart.

Those who have already received their first shot are being encouraged to complete the series for better protection.

Anyone who develops unexplained sores or a suspicious rash should contact a healthcare provider about testing, which typically involves swabbing an affected lesion.

People who suspect they have mpox should avoid close physical contact and sharing personal belongings until they receive medical guidance.

Stanislaus County health officials are currently working alongside the California Department of Public Health and healthcare providers to track the infections and prevent additional cases.

A potentially dangerous strain of mpox has surfaced in California’s Central Valley, with health officials investigating whether the virus is spreading within the US.

Four recent cases of Clade I mpox have been reported in Stanislaus County, raising fresh concerns about possible community transmission of a strain historically associated with international travel.

The California Department of Public Health has confirmed two infections as Clade I, while additional testing is underway to determine whether the remaining two cases involve the same strain, according to Stanislaus County health officials.

Three of the infected individuals reported no recent international travel, while investigators are still examining the travel history of the fourth patient.

The troubling discovery comes as health authorities investigate a possible shift in how the virus is spreading across the country.

Until recently, Clade I mpox infections in the US were largely associated with people who had traveled internationally. But since August 2026, health officials have identified an increasing number of cases involving patients with no recent overseas travel.

That pattern suggests the virus may now be circulating within US communities, although officials have not established how the individuals in Stanislaus County contracted the infection.

Still, Dr. Thea Papasozomenos, Stanislaus County’s public health officer, stressed that the threat to the broader public remains small.

“While we have identified four cases in our county, we want residents to know that the risk to the general public remains low,” Papasozomenos said. “Being aware of the symptoms, getting vaccinated if at risk of exposure to mpox, and seeking medical care when needed are important ways to protect yourself and prevent the spread of mpox.”

Mpox, formerly known as monkeypox, is a viral infection that can cause painful, blister-like sores and a range of flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headaches and muscle aches.

Some patients develop only a handful of lesions without experiencing other symptoms, making infections potentially harder to recognize.

Symptoms can emerge up to 21 days after exposure, and most infected people recover within two to four weeks. However, the disease can sometimes cause serious complications.

There are two major types of the virus, Clade I and Clade II, both of which spread through similar forms of close contact.

The virus is primarily transmitted through direct skin-to-skin contact, including intimate or sexual contact, as well as exposure to infected sores or bodily fluids.

People can also become infected by sharing contaminated clothing, towels or bedding.

However, officials emphasized that the mpox virus does not spread easily through everyday encounters, such as passing someone at a grocery store or sharing an office.

Health authorities are urging residents at increased risk of exposure to get vaccinated with JYNNEOS, a two-dose vaccine administered approximately four weeks apart.

Those who have already received their first shot are being encouraged to complete the series for better protection.

Anyone who develops unexplained sores or a suspicious rash should contact a healthcare provider about testing, which typically involves swabbing an affected lesion.

People who suspect they have mpox should avoid close physical contact and sharing personal belongings until they receive medical guidance.

Stanislaus County health officials are currently working alongside the California Department of Public Health and healthcare providers to track the infections and prevent additional cases.
